prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "ALTRIA GROUP, INC." (ticker MO), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "MO", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Altria Group, Inc.
markets: US moist smokeless tobacco and snus

mission.statement: Responsibly lead the transition of adult smokers to a smoke-free future.
mission.source: Altria 2025 proxy statement (published as the company's Vision, alongside its 'Moving Beyond Smoking' framing)
mission.plain: Keep selling to adult smokers while trying to move them from cigarettes to less harmful smoke-free products.

about.plain: Altria makes and sells cigarettes in the United States, most famously Marlboro. It also sells chewing tobacco like Copenhagen and Skoal, nicotine pouches called on!, and cigars. It owns the NJOY vape brand and a stake in beer maker AB InBev. Fewer people smoke every year, but it keeps raising prices, so it still earns a lot of money.
about.customers: Adult smokers and nicotine users in the US, who buy through convenience stores, gas stations and other retailers supplied by wholesalers.
about.everyday: Marlboro, the red-and-white cigarette pack sold behind the counter of almost every US gas station, is its brand.

money.plain: Marlboro and other cigarettes, Black & Mild cigars
Copenhagen, Skoal dip and on! pouches
small tobacco-free pouches put under the lip
NJOY vapes, bought in 2023; ACE pulled after a patent ruling

result.summary: Altria has a durable but shrinking moat: Marlboro still holds about 40% of US cigarettes and nearly 60% of the premium segment, and heavy regulation, marketing bans and the 1998 settlement make it very hard for a new cigarette rival to emerge, letting it raise prices every year. The weakness is that the moat protects a declining product; its push into smoke-free products has been far less successful than Philip Morris International's ZYN and IQOS, with NJOY ACE blocked by a patent ruling and $2.1B of e-vapor write-downs in 2025.

pricingPower.evidence: In 2025 domestic cigarette shipments fell 10.0% yet smokeable net revenues fell only 3.4% thanks to higher pricing, and smokeable operating income rose to $10,984M from $10,821M; in Q2 2026 smokeable revenues net of excise rose 2.0% while shipments fell 3.2%. Limits are showing: industry discount share rose to 31.8% in 2025 (33.8% in Q2 2026) and Marlboro share slipped from 41.7% to 40.5%.

moats.evidence: Marlboro had a 40.5% share of all US cigarettes and 59.4% of the premium segment in 2025; Copenhagen and Skoal are long-standing leaders in moist smokeless tobacco.
Nicotine dependence and brand habit keep smokers loyal to a brand, though nothing stops a smoker trading down to a discount brand, as rising discount share (31.8% in 2025) shows.
Tobacco products gain no value from more users.

As the largest US cigarette maker (45.2% total retail share in 2025) it spreads manufacturing, distribution and compliance costs over the most volume, earning a 62.4% adjusted operating margin in 2025.

A shrinking, heavily taxed and regulated US cigarette market dominated by Altria, Reynolds American (BAT) and ITG Brands offers no reason for a new entrant, and the 1998 Master Settlement Agreement and FDA rules raise the bar further.
Altria is the incumbent being counter-positioned against by smoke-free products such as PMI's ZYN and illicit disposable vapes.
It has deep experience with FDA product applications and retail trade programs, but its smoke-free efforts have trailed rivals and NJOY ACE was barred by an ITC patent exclusion order.

It owns the US rights to Marlboro, and the FDA's slow authorisation process (Altria sued the FDA in 2026 over review delays) means existing authorised products and grandfathered brands are hard to replicate.

customers.evidence: Marlboro keeps about 59-60% of the premium segment, showing strong loyalty among premium smokers, but overall share is eroding (Marlboro 43.0% in 2020 to 40.5% in 2025) as consumers trade down to discount brands and move to rival smoke-free products; on!'s share of nicotine pouches fell from 18.8% to 15.4% in 2025.

talent.evidence: Altria offers well-paid, stable jobs in Richmond, Virginia, with about 5,900 employees at end-2025, but the tobacco stigma limits its appeal to top talent and it is not a fixture of major best-employer rankings.

product.evidence: Marlboro is the benchmark US premium cigarette, but in smoke-free products Altria trails: ZYN leads nicotine pouches over on!, NJOY ACE was removed after an ITC patent ruling, and it sold its US IQOS rights to PMI in 2024 for $2.7B.

competitors.name: British American Tobacco (Reynolds American)
competitors.note: Reynolds sells Newport, Camel and Pall Mall cigarettes, Grizzly dip, Velo pouches and Vuse vapes, Altria's main rival in nearly every US category.

competitors.name: Philip Morris International
competitors.note: ZYN leads US nicotine pouches against on!, and PMI now sells IQOS heated tobacco in the US after buying the rights from Altria in 2024.

competitors.name: Imperial Brands (ITG Brands)
competitors.note: ITG sells Winston, Kool and Maverick cigarettes, blu vapes and cigars in the US; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Japan Tobacco (Vector Group / Liggett, Logic)
competitors.note: Owns Liggett's discount cigarettes (Eagle 20's, Pyramid) after acquiring Vector Group in 2024, and Logic vapes; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Juul Labs
competitors.note: Private e-cigarette maker that competes with NJOY and has brought patent claims against NJOY products.

competitors.name: Turning Point Brands
competitors.note: Stoker's chewing tobacco, Zig-Zag papers and FRE nicotine pouches.

competitors.name: Swisher International
competitors.note: Private maker of Swisher Sweets cigars and smokeless products competing with Black & Mild.

competitors.name: Scandinavian Tobacco Group
competitors.note: Cigars and pipe tobacco in the US; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Illicit disposable vape makers (Geek Bar and others)
competitors.note: Mostly Chinese unauthorised flavoured disposables, which Altria says make up the majority of the US e-vapor category and draw smokers away from cigarettes and NJOY.

estimates.name: Illicit disposable vape makers (Geek Bar and others)

threats: Accelerating cigarette volume declines (domestic shipments down 10.0% in 2025) that pricing may no longer offset as smokers trade down to discount brands (31.8% share in 2025).

Losing the smoke-free transition to PMI's ZYN and IQOS and to illicit disposable vapes; on!'s pouch share fell to 15.4% in 2025 and NJOY ACE remains off the market after an ITC patent exclusion order.
FDA regulation, including the proposed rule to cap nicotine in cigarettes, and slow or adverse product authorisations.
Excise tax increases and litigation, including Engle progeny and other smoking-and-health cases.
High debt ($24.6B at June 2026) and negative shareholders' equity, with most cash flow committed to the dividend.

ceo.name: Sal Mancuso
ceo.background: Career finance executive who joined Philip Morris USA in 1990, held strategy, finance and compliance roles, and was Altria's CFO from 2020 until becoming CEO in May 2026.

c1.evidence: Altria leads US cigarettes, a mature industry in long-term decline, with domestic cigarette shipments down 10.0% in 2025.

c2.evidence: Smokers choose Marlboro for its brand (59.4% of the premium segment in 2025), an advantage that has lasted decades, but rising discount share and weak smoke-free share show it is eroding.

c3.evidence: Marlboro is one of the world's best-known brands and the default US premium cigarette, but the Altria name is less known and few customers would 'recommend' a cigarette.

c4.evidence: It repeatedly emphasises its vision to 'responsibly lead the transition of adult smokers to a smoke-free future', but most profit still comes from cigarettes and its 2028 US smoke-free goals are being reassessed.

c6.evidence: “Marlboro, cigarettes, Big Tobacco, dividends”: outside the investor community the impression is mostly negative because of smoking's health harm.

c7.evidence: Its core US cigarette market is shrinking, and the growing smoke-free segments are crowded with stronger rivals such as ZYN and illicit vapes.

c8.evidence: It is pushing into nicotine pouches (on! PLUS reached 120,000 stores by mid-2026), e-vapor (NJOY) and non-nicotine (Proper Wild in over 25,000 stores), but is confined to the US after its 2008 spin-off of PMI.

m1.evidence: Sal Mancuso, a career finance executive and former CFO, has focused on executing the existing smoke-free strategy and earnings guidance rather than setting out a new vision.

m2.evidence: Mancuso is a hired professional manager who joined Philip Morris USA in 1990 and became CEO in May 2026, not a founder.

m4.evidence: There is no clear public evidence either way about a servant-leadership style at Altria under Mancuso.

m5.evidence: Altria's culture is disciplined and cost-focused, but its innovation record is weak: it bought JUUL and NJOY stakes rather than inventing, and wrote off most of the JUUL investment.

m6.evidence: Mancuso's background is in finance, strategy and compliance, not engineering or product development.

m7.evidence: Management frames its strategy around moving adult smokers to potentially less harmful products, but the company still earns most of its profit from cigarettes.

m7b.evidence: There is no record of Sal Mancuso giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Mancuso keeps a low public profile typical of a corporate finance executive.

m9.evidence: As CFO since 2020 he helped deliver steady adjusted EPS growth (3.6% a year from 2022 to 2025) and dividends, but the period also saw large losses on JUUL and $2.1B of NJOY-related write-downs in 2025.

m10.evidence: Altria runs a lean cost base, with adjusted operating margins of 62.4% in 2025 and ongoing cost-reduction programmes such as the USSTC facilities consolidation.

c10.evidence: Its products are addictive and harmful; smoke-free alternatives may reduce harm for smokers who switch, but it sells only in the US.

p2.evidence: Making cigarettes and pouches is not technically hard; the barriers are regulatory and brand-based rather than technological.

f1.evidence: Revenues net of excise taxes slipped from $20,841M in 2020 to $20,139M in 2025, falling in four of the last five years.

f2.evidence: Gross margin on revenues net of excise rose from 62.5% in 2020 to 72.2% in 2025, but operating margin fell from 52.2% to 49.2% because of 2025 impairments.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 it had $24,577M of debt against $2,367M of cash and negative shareholders' equity of $2,618M, though debt was about 2.0x adjusted EBITDA.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow rose from $8,385M in 2020 to $9,290M in 2025, but operating income fell from $10,873M to $9,899M after impairments.

v1.evidence: Marlboro is the clear US premium cigarette leader with nearly 60% of the segment, but in nicotine pouches and vapes rivals such as ZYN are the category leaders.

v2.evidence: Altria does not appear on major best-places-to-work lists such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For, and the tobacco stigma weighs on its employer reputation.

c5.evidence: If Altria vanished, adult smokers would switch to other brands and retailers would lose a big product line, but the world's health would arguably improve.
